lessons.title: The Accounting Equation
lessons.chapterTitle: Why Accounting Matters to Oracle Consultants

slots.practicalActivity: Write the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) from memory. Then invent a fictional company, Harrowgate Supply Co., and take 5 real business events for it (for example: owner invests $20,000 cash, the company buys $5,000 of equipment on credit, the company pays $1,200 rent) and show, for each one, exactly how it keeps the equation in balance by listing which side(s) change and by how much.
slots.deliverable: A 5-event worksheet showing the accounting equation staying in balance after each transaction, with before/after totals for Assets, Liabilities, and Equity.

lessons.title: Businesses, Entities and the Books
lessons.chapterTitle: Why Accounting Matters to Oracle Consultants

slots.practicalActivity: Research the legal entity structure of one real public company using its 10-K or investor-relations site -- note whether it reports as a single consolidated entity or lists multiple subsidiaries/legal entities. Write 3-4 sentences explaining why an Oracle Fusion implementation for that company would need more than one 'set of books' (ledger) if it has multiple legal entities.
slots.deliverable: A short written analysis of a real company's legal-entity structure and why it would require multiple Oracle Fusion ledgers.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the normal-balance table from memory for all 5 account types (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Revenue, Expenses), marking which side -- debit or credit -- is normal for each. Then for 6 fictional transactions at Harrowgate Supply Co. (for example: buys inventory on credit, pays an employee's salary, receives cash from a customer), identify which accounts are involved and whether each one increases or decreases, without yet writing the full entry.
slots.deliverable: A completed 5-account-type normal-balance table, plus a 6-transaction worksheet identifying accounts and their direction of change.

slots.practicalActivity: Draw T-accounts for Cash, Accounts Receivable, and Accounts Payable. Post 5 of the transactions from the previous slot into the correct T-accounts (debit side or credit side), and calculate each account's ending balance by hand.
slots.deliverable: 3 completed T-accounts with postings from 5 real transactions and a correctly calculated ending balance for each.

lessons.title: Recording a Transaction Step by Step

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's exact four-step method -- identify the accounts involved, classify each, determine the direction of change, apply the normal-balance rule -- record 5 original journal entries for Harrowgate Supply Co. Include at least one cash transaction, one on-account (credit) transaction, and one loan transaction, modeled on the lesson's own worked examples.
slots.deliverable: 5 correctly formatted journal entries (Debit/Credit lines, balanced amounts) with the four-step reasoning written out for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Take 3 of your own journal entries from the previous slot and deliberately introduce one common mistake into each -- swap debit/credit, post to the wrong account type, or post a one-sided entry. Write what specific symptom each mistake would produce when you build a trial balance, then correct each entry back to its original, correct form.
slots.deliverable: 3 before/after journal-entry pairs, each showing an intentionally introduced mistake, its trial-balance symptom, and the corrected entry.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Debits and Credits: record 5 new original transactions end-to-end for Harrowgate Supply Co. using the four-step method, post every one into T-accounts, calculate ending balances, and total the debit and credit columns across all affected accounts to confirm they are equal -- simulating the full debit/credit cycle from transaction to balanced books.
slots.deliverable: One complete worked example: 5 original journal entries, their postings into T-accounts, and a column total proving debits equal credits.

slots.practicalActivity: Define assets and liabilities in your own words. Then pull 10 real balance-sheet line items from an actual public company's 10-K or annual report (for example 'Cash and cash equivalents', 'Accounts payable', 'Long-term debt') and classify each as either an asset or a liability, further splitting the assets into current vs. non-current based on what that filing shows.
slots.deliverable: A 10-item classification table built from a real company's actual financial filing, splitting each line as asset or liability and current vs. non-current where applicable.

slots.practicalActivity: Define equity and revenue in your own words. Find the same real public company's income statement and balance sheet (via its 10-K or investor-relations site) and extract its total revenue for the most recent period and the equity section's major line items (for example common stock, retained earnings). Write 2-3 sentences on how that company's revenue for the year connects to the change in its retained earnings.
slots.deliverable: Extracted real revenue and equity figures from a public company's actual financial statements, plus a short written explanation of how revenue flows into retained earnings.

slots.practicalActivity: From the same real company's income statement used in the previous slot, list at least 5 actual expense line items it reports (for example cost of revenue, research and development, selling/general/administrative), and classify each as either a direct cost of producing revenue or an operating expense, explaining your reasoning for the 2 hardest-to-classify ones.
slots.deliverable: A 5-item real expense classification table with written reasoning for 2 judgment-call items.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 original journal entries for Harrowgate Supply Co. covering at least one revenue transaction and one expense transaction. Then write one adjusting entry (for example, accruing an unpaid utility bill at month-end) and its corresponding reversing entry for the start of the next period, explaining in one sentence why the reversal is needed.
slots.deliverable: 4 original journal entries plus a matched adjusting/reversing entry pair with a written explanation of the reversal's purpose.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram the relationship between the general ledger and at least 2 subledgers (for example Accounts Payable and Accounts Receivable), showing which subledger transactions ultimately post to which GL account. Then build a full trial balance from the ending balances of every account you have posted across this chapter's exercises so far, confirming the debit and credit column totals match exactly.
slots.deliverable: A GL-to-subledger relationship diagram and one completed trial balance with matching debit/credit column totals from your own posted transactions.

lessons.title: Finding Errors in a Trial Balance

slots.practicalActivity: Take your balanced trial balance from the previous slot and deliberately introduce a $450 transposition error into one account's balance so the columns no longer match. Use the lesson's two division tricks -- divide the difference by 9, then by 2 -- to diagnose the likely error type, then walk through the lesson's 5-step systematic approach to actually locate and fix it.
slots.deliverable: A deliberately broken trial balance, written diagnostic work using both division tricks, and the corrected, re-balanced trial balance.

slots.practicalActivity: For 4 original transactions of your own (one cash sale, one sale on credit, one prepaid customer deposit, one subscription billed monthly), record each one two ways: once under cash-basis accounting and once under accrual-basis accounting, noting in which period revenue would actually be recognized under each method and why they differ.
slots.deliverable: 4 transactions each recorded under both cash-basis and accrual-basis accounting, with the recognition-timing difference explained for each.

lessons.title: Accounting Periods and the Close Cycle

slots.practicalActivity: Lay out a fictional company's monthly close calendar with at least 5 steps, from period-end cutoff through to a final trial balance. Then write 3 original adjusting entries covering an accrual, a deferral, and a prepaid expense being recognized, explaining which accounting period each one affects.
slots.deliverable: A 5-step month-end close calendar plus 3 original adjusting entries (accrual, deferral, prepaid) with the affected period noted for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Calculate straight-line depreciation by hand for a $24,000 piece of equipment with a 4-year useful life and no salvage value, and write the journal entry for one year's depreciation expense. Then record a foreign-currency transaction (for example a $10,000 invoice billed in EUR that is paid later once the exchange rate has moved) and calculate the resulting foreign-currency gain or loss.
slots.deliverable: A completed straight-line depreciation schedule with one year's journal entry, plus one foreign-currency transaction with its gain/loss calculated and journalized.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the accounts and balances built up across this course's exercises for Harrowgate Supply Co., assemble a complete income statement (revenue minus expenses equals net income) for one period. Then assemble a balance sheet as of that period's end, confirming it balances (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) by rolling your net income into Retained Earnings.
slots.deliverable: One complete original income statement and one complete original balance sheet for the same fictional company and period, tying net income into the balance sheet's equity section.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a simple cash flow statement for Harrowgate Supply Co.'s period, splitting your transactions into Operating, Investing, and Financing activities. Then write a one-page walkthrough tracing one specific transaction end-to-end -- from its original journal entry, through the trial balance, into its final resting place on the income statement or balance sheet -- and close with a short written summary, in your own words, of the full month-end/year-end close cycle covered across this course.
slots.deliverable: A completed 3-section cash flow statement, a one-page single-transaction traceability walkthrough, and a written summary of the close cycle.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can record balanced journal entries using debits and credits, build and troubleshoot a trial balance, and produce a basic income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement from a set of transactions -- the accounting foundation every Oracle Fusion Financials configuration decision in this path rests on.
